title: Backup transport verification: deterministic partial-write and interruption tests
value: Make the send-all promise demonstrable under short writes, interrupted system calls and peer failure, so a green network test actually validates transport behavior.
why_now: Catch-up for November 14, actually reviewed and published on November 16. Sources describe their current commits, not a review performed on the missed date. This is the verification portion of the existing November 12/13 send-all proposal, dependent on the primitive being implemented. The unchanged test only checks buffer initialization. The Makefile already discovers test binaries and Ubuntu CI invokes make test, providing a concrete integration path. This has stronger immediate failure-detection value than the two alternative usability projects. Source inspection does not prove CI passes; no C suite was run and no predecessor packet is marked complete.
effort: About 1-2 hours after the send-all implementation, with POSIX socket and test-seam work.
steps: Keep an actual socketpair integration test with a receiver running concurrently. Include a payload larger than normal socket buffers and a bounded timeout so a regression fails instead of hanging.

Introduce a narrowly scoped test seam for the send call, leaving the production default as the real syscall. Script a short write, EINTR, and further short writes, capturing requested offsets and byte counts.

Add deterministic zero-progress and permanent-error sequences, with an error after partial progress. Assert termination and documented error propagation; do not rely on network timing to provoke these cases.

Keep receiver observations independent of sender return values and compare binary bytes exactly. Add peer-disconnect and zero-length checks, clean up descriptors/threads on failure, and run through existing make test and CI without weakening checks.
acceptance_checks: The scripted sequence proves that offsets advance exactly once for accepted bytes and remain unchanged across EINTR; no bytes are dropped or duplicated.
The real receiver obtains a large binary payload exactly, with no socket-buffer deadlock and with a bounded overall test duration.
Zero progress, permanent error and disconnected-peer cases fail predictably; a deliberately broken one-send implementation or the current success-only stub fails the relevant tests.
The tests are included by the current Makefile discovery, existing checks remain enabled, and actual supported-platform test results are recorded during implementation.

evidence.observation: Reviewed November 16: src is explicitly described as implementation skeletons and stubs; the README documents reliable byte framing, Linux/macOS builds, and make test.
Reviewed November 16: network_send_all must loop until count bytes are transferred; network_send_line must format a text line and append a newline. Both return zero on success and minus one on error.
Reviewed November 16: both send functions ignore their arguments and unconditionally return zero. The file includes stdarg.h but network_send_line does not format or send anything.
Reviewed November 16: the only checks initialize recv_buf_t and assert zero length/start. No socket is created and neither send function is exercised.
Reviewed November 16: tests/test_% links common sources and lock_table.c with pthread flags; make test discovers test_*.c binaries and stops when a test returns failure.

Reviewed November 16: Ubuntu CI installs build dependencies, runs a canary check, builds with make all, then invokes make test. This is workflow configuration, not evidence that CI passed in this review.

Current source inspected November 16 converts W and unpacks its shape without explicit channel validation. Its README documents assumed-valid matrices; the separately inspected tests cover valid analytic channels, not a custom-input CLI.

Current main inspected November 16 uses Processes.txt, a fixed quantum of 10, and unconditional chart generation. The README confirms a file-driven interactive workflow, so a configurable headless runner remains useful.

alternatives.title: Build the outstanding validated custom-channel runner
alternatives.reason_not_selected: Impact: lets numerical users supply safe custom inputs. Effort: roughly 2-4 hours. Evidence is strong from the README, solver and numerical tests; however, this repeats the existing channel-runner backlog while the backup transport currently reports success without transferring data. No completion of that earlier proposal is assumed.

alternatives.title: Expose input selection and a headless metrics mode
alternatives.reason_not_selected: Impact: easier reproducible classroom runs. Effort: roughly 2-4 hours plus checking expected scheduling outputs. The entry-point limitation is confirmed, but output correctness needs further behavioral verification. The backup networking contracts give a smaller, more direct implementation and test boundary.
